title: Parts and Wholes
objectives: I can describe a system by naming its components and how they connect.
I can explain how feedback and regulation keep a system steady.
I can tell the difference between a process, a cycle, and a mechanism.
I can write about how the parts of a system depend on one another.
rationale: Systems thinking links science (the body, ecosystems, the water cycle), civics (government and services), and technology (networks and machines). Students need nouns for the parts and shapes of a system (system, component, mechanism, network, cycle, process), a word for the loop that keeps it steady (feedback) and the verb for what the loop does (regulate), and two adjectives for how parts relate (intricate, interdependent). Four of the nouns carry other meanings students already know, such as a network of friends or a washing-machine cycle, so the unit builds precision by asking what must be true of a technical use. The unit builds on categorize, validate, and multifaceted from earlier work.

words.def: A group of parts that work together as a whole to do a job.
words.ex: The body's digestive system breaks food into pieces small enough to be absorbed.
words.ex2: Our school's recycling system works only if every classroom sorts its trash correctly.
words.nonExample: A single loose screw lying on a table is not a system.

passage.title: The Body's Thermostat
paras: Your body is a system, a group of components that work together to do something no single part could do alone. One job of this system is keeping your temperature steady, near 37 degrees Celsius, whether you are on a sunny beach or waiting for a bus in the snow. The body does not leave this to chance.

The key mechanism works much like the thermostat in a house. Sensors in your skin and brain detect changes in temperature and send signals along a network of nerves to a control center in the brain. That center compares what it receives with a target range and decides whether the body needs to cool down or warm up.

If you overheat, blood vessels near the skin widen and the sweat glands release moisture. As the sweat evaporates, it carries heat away. If you get cold, the vessels narrow and the muscles shiver, which produces heat. Each response is a process made of several steps, and each ends when the temperature is back in the right range.

That ending depends on feedback. The sensors keep reporting, so when your temperature moves toward normal, the control center eases off the response. This is how the body can regulate its temperature without any thought from you. The components are interdependent: sweat glands cannot cool you unless blood carries heat to the skin, and nerves cannot act unless the muscles and glands answer.

The whole arrangement is intricate, with countless small adjustments happening every minute, and it works as a cycle of sensing, signaling, responding, and rechecking. The next time you shiver or sweat, remember that it is not a flaw. It is evidence that a well-built system is doing its job.

qs.q: In paragraph 4, the word “interdependent” most nearly means
qs.why: The sentence says sweat glands cannot cool you unless blood carries heat, so each part needs the others.

qs.q: Which detail best shows feedback at work?
choices: Sensors in the skin and brain detect temperature changes.
The sensors keep reporting, so the control center eases off as temperature nears normal.
qs.why: Feedback is information about results that adjusts what happens next, and the easing off is that adjustment.

qs.q: Why does the author compare the body to a thermostat?
choices: To show that the body is made of metal parts
To argue that houses are healthier than bodies
To explain a control mechanism that senses and corrects temperature
To describe how heat travels through walls
qs.why: A thermostat senses temperature and switches heat on or off, which matches what the body's control center does.

qs.q: What would most likely happen if the nerves between the skin and the brain stopped carrying signals?
choices: Body temperature would stay perfect with no effort.
The sensors would no longer be needed.
The control center would not learn about temperature changes, so the response would be weaker or late.
qs.why: The passage says signals travel along nerves to the control center, so without them the center would lack the information it uses.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: The body keeps its temperature steady through connected parts and feedback.
Sweating is the most important thing the body does.
Shivering shows that a person is sick.
Thermostats were designed by copying the body.
qs.why: The passage describes sensors, a control center, responses, and feedback that together keep temperature steady.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for describing how parts work together, read a science passage about how the body regulates temperature, and write about a system they know. The unit turns the idea of a system into a set of questions: what are the parts, how do they connect, and what keeps them steady?

notes.va.system.n: Start with a concrete system, such as a bicycle, and have students label parts and connections before moving to the body. Watch for the use of system as a synonym for rule.
notes.va.component.n: A component is a part that can be named and has a role. Ask students to name three components of a school lunch line. A frequent error is calling a whole thing a component of itself.
notes.va.mechanism.n: A mechanism explains how, not just what. Pair with a picture of a lock and ask students to say what moves, then what that moves. The family includes mechanical and mechanic.
notes.va.network.n: Contrast the shapes: a chain has one path, a network has many. Show the computer sense briefly, since students use it already. Ask what is lost if one connection breaks.
notes.va.cycle.n: A cycle returns to its start. Use the cycle diagram and have students add arrows. The bicycle sense is shown to explain the cyc root; do not push morphology beyond that.
notes.va.feedback.n: Feedback is information about results that changes what happens next. Distinguish from comments given at the end, with no way to adjust. Use a thermostat and a coach as two examples.
notes.va.process.n: A process has steps and ends in a result. Have students describe making toast or doing laundry as a process with time-order words. The verb sense (to process data or food) is shown for recognition.
notes.va.regulate.v: Regulate means keep within limits. Contrast with control (which can mean stop) and stop. Students will see two sets of examples, such as body temperature and laws.
notes.va.intricate.adj: Intricate is about fine, carefully arranged detail, not just difficulty. A difficult but plain task is not intricate. Use a snowflake or a spider web photo.
notes.va.interdependent.adj: Build the word from inter- plus depend plus -ent. The key idea is mutual need. Ask for an example that is dependent in only one direction, to show the contrast.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: “The text calls the body a system. I look for the components: sensors, nerves, a control center, sweat glands, and muscles. They send signals through a network of nerves, so the parts are connected. I notice that the sensors keep reporting even after the body responds, and that is feedback. It shows how the system keeps itself steady.”
discuss: Which systems in your life depend on feedback, and what happens when it goes wrong?
How is a network different from a cycle, and can one system have both?
misconceptions: A system is any group of things.
A mechanism is always a machine.
A cycle and a process are the same thing.
extend: Draw and label a system from another class, such as a food web, a watershed, or the school bus network, marking each component and one feedback loop.
Write a paragraph that explains how a human body system and a machine are alike and different, using at least five unit words.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Link back to categorize, validate, and multifaceted by asking students to categorize the components of a system, validate a claim about how it works, and decide whether it is multifaceted. Revisit system, feedback, and interdependent two days later in a labeling task, again at one week with a new system, and in the conflict unit when students describe how disputes escalate.

needsReview: Passage facts to confirm with a science reviewer: normal body temperature near 37 degrees Celsius; skin and brain sensors with a brain control center; blood vessels widen to release heat and narrow in cold; shivering produces heat; sweat evaporating carries heat away.
Example facts to confirm: geckos climbing glass, bees finding their way to the hive, the water cycle, the moon's phases repeating about monthly, snowflake structure.
Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: retroalimentación (feedback; realimentación is used in some regions), red (network), intrincado, regular (regulate), clasificar not used here.
Sense boundary: network, cycle, and process list a second sense in senses; check that each example uses the intended sense.
